title: Quality Control & SPC
summary: Cp/Cpk process capability, X-bar & R control charts, common vs special cause, and the Six Sigma ppm scale for production quality.

sections.heading: Quality Is Process, Not Inspection
sections.content: Inspection finds bad parts; **quality control** prevents them. The shift is statistical: every process has natural variation, and the job of SPC is to distinguish the *normal* spread from a *changing* process — and to act on the change before bad parts exist. The two questions of quality engineering: *Can this process hold the tolerance?* (capability) and *Is the process staying on target?* (control). Capability is designed in; control is managed daily.

sections.heading: Cp & Cpk: Can the Process Hold It?
sections.content:
Capability compares the **specification width** to the **natural process spread** (6σ, which contains ~99.7% of a normal process):

$$C_p = \frac{USL - LSL}{6\sigma}$$

$C_p$ measures spread only — it says nothing about centering. The centered version:

$$C_{pk} = \min\left(\frac{USL - \bar{x}}{3\sigma}, \frac{\bar{x} - LSL}{3\sigma}\right)$$

Example — spec 10 ± 0.1 mm (USL = 10.1, LSL = 9.9), sample σ = 0.03 mm, mean = 10.02 mm:

$$C_p = \frac{0.2}{6 \times 0.03} = 1.11, \qquad C_{pk} = \min\left(\frac{0.08}{0.09}, \frac{0.12}{0.09}\right) = \min(0.89, 1.33) = 0.89$$

The process spread is fine ($C_p = 1.11$) but **off-center** ($C_{pk} = 0.89 < 1$): ~0.4% of parts exceed the upper limit. Industry norms: $C_{pk} \geq 1.33$ for normal production (0.1 ppm at 4σ), 1.67 for safety-critical. A capability study is only valid for a **stable** (in-control) process — capability measured on an uncontrolled process is fiction.

sections.heading: X-bar & R Control Charts
sections.content:
Control charts track the process over time. For variables (measured dimensions), the pair is **X-bar** (mean of subgroups) and **R** (range within subgroup):

$$CL_{X} = \bar{\bar{x}} \pm A_2 \bar{R}, \qquad CL_R = D_3 \bar{R} \text{ to } D_4 \bar{R}$$

($A_2$, $D_3$, $D_4$ are constants from subgroup size.) The chart is read for **signals**:

- One point beyond 3σ control limits — likely special cause (tool wear spike, material change).
- **Run of 7+ points** on one side of the center line, or 7 rising/falling — drift, not noise (tool wear ramping, coolant temperature).
- Other runs tests (2 of 3 beyond 2σ, 4 of 5 beyond 1σ) add sensitivity at the cost of alarms.

The rule: **common cause** variation (inherent, stable) is reduced by process *improvement*; **special cause** variation (assignable — a crashed insert, a new batch, a mis-set fixture) is removed by *action*. Charting without acting on special causes is theater.

sections.heading: Control & Capability Are Different
sections.content:
A process can be **in control but out of spec** — tight, stable, and wrong: the classic case of a process centered at the wrong nominal with $C_{pk} < 1$. Conversely, a process can be in spec on average yet out of control — unstable, drifting within the limits until it doesn't.

The hierarchy: first **remove special causes** (stabilize the chart), then **improve the common-cause spread** (process change: better tooling, material, method — see [[machining-fundamentals|machining]] for the lever list), then **re-center** if $C_{pk} < C_p$. Only then quote $C_{pk} \geq 1.33$ with confidence. And remember the measurement system must be sound before any of this means anything (see [[metrology-and-inspection|gauge R&R]]).

sections.heading: The Six Sigma Scale
sections.content:
The Six Sigma movement formalized a defect scale. With a 1.5σ mean shift allowed (the standard assumption), process spread vs expected defect rate:

| Process level (spread) | ppm out of spec |
|---|---|
| ±1σ | 317 000 |
| ±2σ | 45 500 |
| ±3σ | 2 700 |
| ±4σ | 63 |
| ±5σ | 0.57 |
| ±6σ | 0.002 (the famous "3.4" with shift) |

Perspective: ±3σ (a Cpk of 1.0 with shift) already means ~2700 defective ppm — visible on any production line. Six Sigma quality is not a moral ideal; it is a **cost decision** about scrap, rework, and warranty, made with exactly these numbers. Most well-managed machining runs land Cpk 1.33–1.67 — the corridor between "competent" and "exceptional".

sections.heading: Sampling, AQL & the Inspection Strategy
sections.content:
Control charts earn their keep by **reducing inspection**:

- A **capable, in-control** process needs only sampling (typically 3–8 pieces per shift with charts) — 100% inspection is a symptom of an uncontrolled process.
- For attribute (go/no-go) checks, **AQL sampling plans** (ISO 2859) fix sample size and acceptance numbers by lot size and AQL level: accepting a 1.0% AQL plan means lots with ≤1% defectives are accepted most of the time.
- **100% inspection** stays justified for safety-critical features, Cpk < 1.0 processes, or where defect cost is huge — but it is ~85–90% effective at best (operator fatigue); automated vision re-raises it.
- The loop closes with **reaction plans**: an out-of-control signal triggers containment (quarantine, 100% check), correction (root cause), and validation — then the chart resumes. Quality is closed-loop, not a report.

keyTakeaways: Capability: Cp = (USL−LSL)/6σ and Cpk vs centering; require Cpk ≥ 1.33 for stable production.
Control charts separate common cause (improve the process) from special cause (act now).
In-control ≠ in-spec: stabilize first, then reduce spread, then re-center.
SPC sampling replaces 100% inspection once the process is capable; close the loop with reaction plans.
